Common year starting on Saturday

A common year starting on Saturday is any non- leap year(i.e. a year with 365 days) that begins on Saturday, 1 January, and ends on Saturday, 31 December. Its dominical letter hence is B. The most recent year of such kind was 2022, and the next one will be 2033 in the Gregorian calendar or, likewise, 2023 and 2034 in the obsolete Julian calendar. See below for more.

Any common year that starts on Saturday has only one Friday the 13th: the only one in this common year occurs in May. Leap years starting on Friday share this characteristic.

## Applicable years

### Gregorian Calendar

In the (currently used) Gregorian calendar, alongside Sunday, Monday, Wednesday or Friday, the fourteen types of year (seven common, seven leap) repeat in a 400-year cycle (20871 weeks). Forty-three common years per cycle or exactly 10.75% start on a Saturday. The 28-year sub-cycle will break at a century year which is not divisible by 400 (e.g. it broke at the year 1900 but not at the year 2000).

### Julian Calendar

In the now-obsolete Julian calendar, the fourteen types of year (seven common, seven leap) repeat in a 28-year cycle(1461 weeks). A leap year has two adjoining dominical letters, (one for January and February and the other for March to December in the Church of England, as 29 February has no letter). Each of the seven two-letter sequences occurs once within a cycle, and every common letter thrice.

As the Julian calendar repeats after 28 years that means it will also repeat after 700 years, i.e. 25 cycles. The year's position in the cycle is given by the formula (((year + 8) mod 28) + 1). Years 10, 16 and 27 of the cycle are common years beginning on Saturday. 2017 is year 10 of the cycle. Approximately 10.71% of all years are common years starting on Saturday.

A common year starting on Saturday is a common year that begins on Saturday, January 1, and ends on Saturday, December 31. Thus, its dominical letter is B. Examples include 1977, 1983, 1994, 2005, 2011, 2022, and 2033 in the Gregorian calendar, or likewise, 1995, 2006, 2017, 2023 and 2034 in the Julian Calendar (see tables below for more).

In this common year, January and October begin on Saturday, February, March, and November begin on Tuesday, April and July begin on Friday, May begins on Sunday, June begins on Wednesday, August begins on Monday, and September and December begin on Thursday. Thus, there are three months that begin on a weekend day. This is one of two common years with this property, the other being Common year starting on Tuesday.

This common year is one of three common years with only one Friday the 13th, the others being Common year starting on Wednesday and Common year starting on Friday. The Friday the 13th in this common year is in May. This characteristic is shared with a Leap year starting on Friday.

This common year is one of three common years with only one Friday the 17th, the others being Common year starting on Monday and Common year starting on Tuesday. The only Friday the 17th in this common year is in June. Leap years starting on Friday share this characteristic.

This common year is one of three common years with two Tuesday the 13ths, the others being Common year starting on Thursday and Common year starting on Friday. The Tuesday the 13ths in this common year are in September and December. Leap years starting on Friday share this characteristic. From July of the year preceding this type of year (either a Leap year starting on Thursday or Common year starting on Friday) is the longest period (14 months) between two instances of Tuesday the 13th. Leap years starting on Wednesday share this characteristic, from August of the year that precedes it (Common year starting on Tuesday) to October in that type of year.

In this common year, Martin Luther King Jr. Day is on January 17, Valentine’s Day is on a Monday, Presidents Day is on its latest possible date, February 21, Daylight Savings Time begins on March 13, St. Patrick’s Day is on a Thursday, Mother’s Day is on its earliest possible date, May 8, Memorial Day is on May 30, Father’s Day is on June 19, Independence Day is on a Monday, Labor Day is on September 5, Columbus Day is on October 10, Halloween is on a Monday, Daylight Savings Time ends on November 6, Veterans Day is on a Friday, Thanksgiving is on November 24, and Christmas is on a Sunday.

In a 400-year cycle in the Gregorian Calendar, 43 or 10.75% of all years are common years starting on Saturday. Like all common years, they occur in a pattern of 6-11-11 years (e.g. 2005, 2011, 2022, 2033). However, this pattern gets broken when there is a century year that is not a leap year. Over the past 400-year cycle (from 1600 to 2000), there were 6-year gaps between 1689, 1695, 1701 and 1707, a 12-year gap between 1791 and 1803 and another 12-year gap between 1898 and 1910. In the Julian Calendar there are three common years starting on Saturday in a 28-year cycle.

# Common year starting on Saturday

Ara Eve Leo Sal

1x

A common year starting on Saturday is a non-leap year in the Gregorian calendar consisting of exactly 365 days, with January 1 falling on a Saturday and, consequently, December 31 also falling on a Saturday.[1] This configuration arises because a common year comprises 52 full weeks (364 days) plus one additional day, preserving the starting weekday for both the first and last days of the year.[1] In the Gregorian calendar, which is the internationally accepted civil calendar, such years repeat in patterns influenced by the 400-year leap year cycle, typically recurring every 6, 11, or 17 years due to the interplay of common and leap years.[2] Historical and recent examples include 1977, 1983, 1994, 2005, 2011, and 2022, with future occurrences projected for 2033, 2039, and 2050.[2] These years share an identical calendar layout, meaning the days of the week align the same way for all dates, facilitating the reuse of annual planners and schedules.[2] One notable aspect of common years starting on Saturday is the positioning of major holidays and observances. For instance, New Year's Day occurs on a Saturday, while Christmas Day occurs on a Sunday; Easter Sunday varies based on lunar calculations but often aligns with specific weekdays in this calendar type.[3] This alignment can influence workweeks, travel patterns, and cultural events, as weekends bookend the year and certain mid-year dates like July 4(in the United States) fall on a Monday.[3] The Gregorian system's design ensures these patterns contribute to the calendar's overall predictability over long periods.[4]

## Overview and Properties

### Definition and Characteristics

A common year, also known as a non-leap year, in the Gregorian calendar consists of 365 days, comprising 12 months with February having 28 days and no intercalary February 29.[1] This duration equates to exactly 52 weeks and 1 extra day, which shifts the starting weekday of the following year by one day relative to the current year's start.[1] In a common year starting on Saturday, January 1 falls on a Saturday, initiating a sequential progression of weekdays throughout the year, with December 31 also landing on a Saturday due to the alignment of the extra day.[1] The extra day in such a year results in an uneven distribution of weekdays: there are 53 Saturdays and 52 occurrences each of Sunday, Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, and Friday.[5] This pattern arises because the 52 full weeks account for one of each weekday, while the additional day reinforces the starting Saturday. Consequently, the following year begins on Sunday, advancing the calendar by one weekday from the prior year's start.[1] In contrast, a leap year starting on Saturday features 366 days, equivalent to 52 weeks and 2 extra days, leading to 53 Saturdays and 53 Sundays, with 52 of each remaining weekday.[6] This configuration shifts the subsequent year to start on Monday, a two-day advancement due to the leap day.[7] The Doomsday rule can verify these alignments, though detailed computation is addressed elsewhere.

### Calculation Methods

One effective method for identifying common years starting on Saturday is the Doomsday rule, developed by mathematician John H. Conway in the late 20th century. This approach uses memorable "doomsday" dates for each month—such as 4/4 for April, 6/6 for June, 9/5 for September, and 12/12 for December—to anchor calculations within a year. To compute the doomsday (the weekday shared by these dates) for a given year in the Gregorian calendar, first determine the century anchor day: Wednesday for 1900–1999, Tuesday for 2000–2099, Sunday for 2100–2199, and Friday for 1800–1899. Then, for a year YYYY, let y = (YYYY mod 100); the doomsday is the century anchor plus y + ⌊y/4⌋ (mod 7), adding 1 more if the year is a leap year(though for common year s, this extra is omitted). In a common year, January 3 is the doomsday, so January 1 falls two days before the doomsday (mod 7). A year starts on Saturday if its doomsday is Monday, as Saturday+ 2 ≡ Monday(mod 7).[8] A direct formula for the weekday of January 1 in the Gregorian calendar is an adaptation of Zeller's congruence, originally formulated by Christian Zeller in 1883. For January 1 of year YYYY (a common year), treat it as day q = 1 in month m = 13 of the previous year Y = YYYY - 1; let K = Y mod 100 and J = ⌊Y / 100⌋. The weekday h is given by

h=(q+⌊13(m+1)5⌋+K+⌊K4⌋+⌊J4⌋−2J)mod 7, h = \left( q + \left\lfloor \frac{13(m+1)}{5} \right\rfloor + K + \left\lfloor \frac{K}{4} \right\rfloor + \left\lfloor \frac{J}{4} \right\rfloor - 2J \right) \mod 7,

where h = 0 for Saturday, 1 for Sunday, ..., 6 for Friday. To find common years starting on Saturday, solve for YYYY such that h = 0, adjusting for the common-year constraint (YYYY not divisible by 4, or divisible by 100 but not 400). This modular equation allows systematic identification by iterating over years or solving the congruence.[9] A simpler incremental method uses an anchor year with a known starting weekday, such as 1900, which began on Monday in the Gregorian calendar. For a target common year YYYY > 1900, compute the total day shift as (YYYY - 1900) + L mod 7, where L is the number of leap years from 1900 to YYYY - 1, given by ⌊(YYYY - 1)/4⌋ - ⌊(YYYY - 1)/100⌋ + ⌊(YYYY - 1)/400⌋ minus the same for 1899. Add this shift to Monday (coded as 1, with Saturday= 0, mod 7); a result of 0 mod 7 indicates a Saturday start. This method leverages the 365 ≡ 1 (mod 7) property of common years and 366 ≡ 2 (mod 7) for leaps.[10] For verification, apply the Doomsday rule to 2005(a common year): century anchor Tuesday(2), y = 5, doomsday = 2 + 5 + ⌊5/4⌋ = 2 + 5 + 1 = 8 ≡ 1 (Monday) mod 7. If doomsday is Monday, Jan 3 is Monday, so Jan 1 is Saturday(two days before). Historical records confirm January 1, 2005, was a Saturday. The Zeller adaptation and anchor method similarly yield Saturday for 2005.[8][9][10][11]

## Applicable Years

### Gregorian Calendar

In the proleptic Gregorian calendar, common years starting on Saturday occur when January 1 falls on a Saturday and the year has 365 days, adhering to leap year rules where years divisible by 4 are leap except for century years not divisible by 400. The calendar's structure ensures patterns repeat every 28 years in most cases due to the solar cycle, where 28 years encompass 10227 days (28 × 365 + 7 leap days), equivalent to exactly 1461 weeks, aligning weekdays with dates; however, exceptions arise every 100 years when a century year skips a leap day (unless divisible by 400), shifting the cycle within the overall 400-year repeat of 146097 days (20871 weeks).[12] The condition for such years can be determined using the formula for the cumulative days modulo 7: (year + ⌊year/4⌋ - ⌊year/100⌋ + ⌊year/400⌋) mod 7 = 6, derived from Zeller's congruence adapted for January 1, where this value corresponds to Saturday based on verified examples like 1994 and 2022; leap years are excluded by checking divisibility rules.[9] This pattern holds proleptically from the calendar's 1582 introduction, with examples in the late 16th century including 1583 and 1594.

These 21 years represent the occurrences within the 200-year span from 1901 to 2100, averaging about one every 9.5 years due to the interplay of common and leap years advancing the weekday by 1 or 2 days annually. Future projections follow the 28-year repeats with skips at non-leap centuries like 2100, so the next after 2095 is 2106.[3][13][14]

### Julian Calendar

In the Julian calendar, common years starting on Saturday occur within a strict 28-year solar cycle, owing to the calendar's uniform leap year rule where every fourth year is a leap year without exceptions for century years. This cycle comprises 28 years totaling 10,227 days, equivalent to exactly 1,461 weeks, ensuring that the alignment of weekdays with dates repeats precisely every 28 years. Unlike the Gregorian calendar, which introduces irregularities through skipped leap years in most century years, the Julian system's consistency simplifies long-term pattern prediction.[15] To identify such years, an adapted form of Zeller's congruence can be applied specifically for the Julian calendar. For January 1 in a common year(non-leap), compute ((year - 1) + ⌊(year - 1)/4⌋) mod 7; a result of 0 indicates the year begins on Saturday, where the day numbering aligns with standard conventions (0 for Saturday in the base Zeller formulation). Examples from 1 to 100 AD include 1, 7, 18, 29, 35, 46, 57, 63, 74, 85, and 91, with the sequence recurring every 28 years—such as 29, 35, 46, 57, 63, 74, 85, 91, 102, 109, 120 in the following century—extending proleptically up to 2100. These years must also satisfy the common year condition (year not divisible by 4).[16] The Julian calendar, introduced in 45 BC by Julius Caesar, served as the standard civil calendar across the Roman Empire and much of Europe until the late 16th century. It was widely used until 1582, when Pope Gregory XIII's reform led to its replacement in Catholic regions to correct seasonal drift; Protestant and Orthodox areas adopted the Gregorian calendar later, with some Eastern Orthodox churches retaining the Julian for liturgical purposes to this day. Post-1582, the proleptic Julian calendar—extending the system hypothetically forward and backward—facilitates historical and astronomical comparisons.[17] This drift arises because the Julian year's average length of 365.25 days exceeds the tropical year's 365.2422 days, accumulating an extra day approximately every 128 years. By 1582, the discrepancy reached 10 days; it increased to 11 after 1700, 12 after 1800, and 13 after 1900. Consequently, by 2100, Julian dates run 13 days ahead of corresponding Gregorian dates for the same astronomical moment, shifting the weekday alignment between the calendars and requiring adjustments when comparing year-starting days across systems.[17]

## Calendar Layout

### Monthly Day Assignments

In a common year starting on Saturday, the Gregorian calendar assigns specific weekdays to dates across the months, determined by the cumulative number of days from January 1, which falls on a Saturday. Common Year – Standard Year – Normal Year

 

Home Calendar Common Year

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 A common year has 365 days. In a leap year, a day is added.

## A Calendar Year

In our modern-day Gregorian calendar, a common year has 365 days, as opposed to a leap year which has 366 days.

A Gregorian common year consists of 52 weeks and one day. Because of this, January 1 and December 31 of a common year are always on the same day of the week, and the next year begins on the next day of the week. For instance, the common year 2026 starts and ends on a Thursday, and 2027 begins on a Friday.

 Why a week has 7 days (and in that order) 

In leap years, the first and last days fall on different days of the week. 2028 is a leap year. It starts on a Saturday and ended on a Sunday.

Out of every 400 years in the Gregorian calendar, 303 years are common years. The rest, 97 years, have an intercalary day or leap year day, making them 366 days long.

 What is a tropical year? Why Mars has more leap years than Earth 

## Common Years in Other Calendars

### Hebrew Calendar

The Hebrew Calendar, which is a lunisolar calendar, has 12 months in a common year, which can have anywhere from 353 to 355 days. Leap years in such a calendar have 383 to 384 days and 13 months.

### Chinese Calendar

A common year in the Chinese Calendar, which is also a lunisolar calendar, has 12 months with 353–355 days. A month in a Chinese common year corresponds to the cycle of the Moon, from full Moon to full Moon. Because of this, a regular month can have 29 or 30 days. Leap years in the Chinese Calendar have 13 months.

### Islamic Calendar

Common years in the Islamic Calendar, which is purely a lunar calendar, have 354 days divided into 12 months. Some months have 30 days while others have 29 days. 11 out of 30 years are Islamic leap years, where the leap year has 30 days in the last month of the year, making the Islamic leap year 355 days. Different communities follow different rules about how to space the leap years in the 30-year leap cycle.

### Indian Calendar

Both solar and lunisolar calendars are used in India and the Indian subcontinent, each with regional variations. The solar calendar aligns with astronomical calculations for leap years, rather than a fixed cycle. Common years have 365 days, and leap years have 366.

Two kinds of lunisolar calendars, Amanta and Purnimanta, are used in the Indian system. The Amanta calendar counts months from new Moon to new Moon, while the Purnimanta counts from full Moon to full Moon. The common year in the Amanta Calendar is 354 days long, with each month averaging about 29.5 days. To maintain alignment with the solar year, seven intercalary months, called Adhik Maas, are added at different intervals over a 19-year cycle.

results.text:
Common year

A common year is a calendar year with 365 days, as distinguished from a leap year, which has 366 days. More generally, a common year is one without intercalation. The Gregorian calendar, used by the majority of the world, employs both common years and leap years. This is to keep the calendar aligned with the tropical year, which does not contain an exact number of days. A common year is approximately a quarter day (six hours) shorter than a tropical year, which has 365.24 days. If the Gregorian calendar only used common years and omitted leap years, the calendar would be out of sync with the tropical year by approximately 24 days in 100 years.

In the Gregorian calendar, 303 out of every 400 years are common years. Leap years are any years that are divisible by 4, unless it can also be divided by 100, in which case it is a common year. One exception is if the year can be divided by 4, 100, and 400 - these years are leap years. The extra common years are added to account for the fact that common years are 5 hours, 48 minutes, and 46 seconds shorter than a tropical year, rather than six hours exactly. By comparison, in the Julian calendar, 300 out of every 400 years are common years, with every fourth year being a leap year without exception.

The common year has 52 weeks and one day, hence a common year always begins and ends on the same day of the week (for example, January 1 and December 31 both fall on a Thursday in 2026) and the year following a common year will start on the subsequent day of the week. As a result, if the following year is a common year as well, each date will advance by one day of the week. For example, March 1, 2025 fell on a Saturday, then it falls on a Sunday in 2026 and Monday in 2027. If the following year is a leap year, then dates from January 1 to February 28 will still advance by one day, but all subsequent dates will advance by two days (for example, March 1 falls on a Monday in 2027 and Wednesday in 2028), due to the additional day.
